translation:
...was in his service. One day he had gone out to buy vegetables for the ashram kitchen. On the way, some distance off, he saw a saint standing there — the saint simply stood in that same spot. He felt as though his own feet had become locked in place; his feet would not move at all. They would move to go toward the saint, but they would not move to go toward the market. When he reached the saint, he could not help but bow to him. Placing a hand on his head, the saint said, "So you have come at last. My child, I was waiting just for you — now you will not be able to remain apart from me." This saint was Shri Yukteshwar Giri. With the help of Shri Sadguru Yukteshwar Giri, this disciple was able to rise to the stature of Yoganandji Paramahansa, and served as India's representative at the world's parliament of religions. Hence Kabir Saheb rightly says:

_Pahele parche guru mile, duje sarjanhaar ||_
(First, through direct recognition, one attains the guru; through him, second, one attains the Creator.)

If one obtains a guru, one attains the vision of the Supreme Being. He who is the Creator, who is the lord of the world, is that very Parmeshwar; he alone takes care of everyone. Whatever any soul longs for, he brings to that soul sooner or later, in one way or another. When souls feel a spiritual hunger, that same Paramatma sends a sadguru to bring the soul the help it needs. Through the guru's grace, the deep secrets of the spiritual world then open up before that seeking soul. The soul comes to recognize its own true nature. Only after winning the guru's love does the seeking soul obtain the good fortune of the guru's grace; through that, its journey toward the highest good keeps advancing. Then, on some blessed day, through the sadguru's grace, a glimpse of the Supreme Being is attained. It is a well-known fact that Kabir Saheb, too, came to know his sadguru Ramanandji in just this way.

For this reason, experienced and wise men keep singing the glory of the guru. In the guru's company one gets the good fortune of plundering an inexhaustible spiritual treasure. The memory of one's births across many lifetimes stirs and awakens. Within the body a continual sacrifice of purification (shuddhi yajna) keeps going on. Futile activity comes to an end. Thoughts find a definite direction. The mind increasingly takes on wholesome resolve. Restraint over speech keeps growing. The senses come under control. The inner faculty (antahkaran) becomes pure. In this way the ground for the vision of the Supreme Being is laid through the guru's company.

[Kabirvani, Year 10, Issue 114, Bavaji, Kapura, pages 1-5.]

Jagdish of Ravapura had an experience just like this.

Regarding guru and sadguru, the Vaishnav Nana Parekh has written a pad (hymn) in the Sindhudo raga.

_Sindhudo

Bhajat mugat tano swami chhe sahelo | Goheló hoy te shu re aape |
Jaachak hoy te jaacho tehne jai | Dukh daaridray sarve kaape ||tek||

Shuk Samkaadik Aadinaarad dai | Saadh sarve mali mugat maage |
Bhagatinaa bhogiaa sant viralaa koi | Teh kahiye motaa param bhaagi ||1||

Jire guru sadguru biche vaharo atidhano | Guru to vegne mukh bole |
Sadguru bhed bataave samjhaave igam tano | Kot mugat nahi teh tole ||2||

Jire jehne jevo guru male tene tevi ugrataa | Kije udyam tevo laabh lije |
Bhaare halvaa tanu nathi jene paarkhu | Tene dosh te kem dije ||3||

Jivanchaa Prabhu mugat morlidharaa | Gopi tanaa var garuaa kahaave |
Naano sevak kari sant ne sopie | Bhagat daataar bhalaaj bhaavo ||4||

Saakhi
Kabir sadguru guru bich bahu antadaa | Jyon divas aru jaam |
Guru bataave vaikunthaku | Sadguru de nij dhaam ||1||_

(Devotion's very master is gracious and easy of approach — what can a niggard lord give? If you are a fit beggar, go and ask of him — he cuts away every sorrow and every poverty. [refrain] Shuk, Sanakadik, Narad, and all the rest — every seeker joins together and asks for liberation, but rare indeed is the saint who longs to enjoy loving devotion itself; call such a one the greatest of the fortunate. [1] Between guru and sadguru there is a very great gulf: the guru merely speaks urgently with his mouth, while the sadguru shows the hidden secret and explains what is unfathomable — millions of liberations cannot equal that. [2] Whatever kind of guru one obtains, that intensity of practice must be taken up, and the benefit gained accordingly; one who cannot tell heavy from light should not be blamed for it. [3] The Lord of life wears the peacock-feather crown and holds the flute; he is called the great, honored husband of the gopis. Make me the lowliest of servants and hand me over to the saints — devotion is the true giver, may this be granted with grace. [4] Sakhi: Kabir says there is a vast gap between guru and sadguru, as between day and night. The guru shows the way to Vaikunth; the sadguru gives his own abode. [1])

The master of loving devotion and liberation is himself supremely gracious and worthy, but how could a wretched, miserly lord give us happiness? If you are a fit beggar, then go to such a one and ask of him what can cure your sorrows and your poverty. Shukdev, Sanakadik, Narad, and the rest — all seekers alike gather together and, with one mind, ask for liberation; but those who wish to enjoy Hari's loving devotion are only a rare few saints. Them alone shall we call the truly fortunate. Ah, but there is a very great difference between a guru and a sadguru! One who is merely a guru gives instruction only by speaking with his mouth, whereas one who is a sadguru gives understanding of whatever hidden mystery one is unable to grasp on one's own — even millions of liberations cannot equal that. Hence, whatever kind of devotional practice (upasana) a person's guru follows, that guru shows him that same kind of practice with great intensity; but even after millions of labors spent on it, one may still fail to receive the benefit of one's own deliverance through it. As for one who has no discernment of what a superior or an ordinary devotional practice is — for such a one there is Lord Krishna, who wears the crown of peacock feathers and holds the flute, who is called the great, honored husband of the gopis. Surrender yourself, becoming his lowly devotee-servant, and place yourself under the shelter of the saints, for they carry the virtuous, gracious nature that gives loving devotion.

The Sakhi — Das Kabirji says that between guru and sadguru there is a very great difference: just as there is a great distance between day and night, such is the difference between guru and sadguru. A guru merely shows us how to attain a liberated realm such as Vaikunth, while a sadguru shows us how to attain his own divine abode (Bhagavad-dhaam).

Trikamdas Gordhandas has written a kundali (expanded verse) on guru and sadguru. [Diary of Samvat] 2032, page 15.

_Guru sadguru bahu aantaro | Jyu divas jharu jaam |
Guru bataave vaikunthaku | Sadguru de nij dhaam ||
Sadguru de nij dhaam | Talee jaay janamnaa feraa |
Shaa inth aan | Akhand Vrundavan heraa |
Trikam sadguru vachane aaraam | Ghar bethaan chhe jaataraa |
Jyu divas aru jaam | Guru sadguru bahu aantaro ||_

(Between guru and sadguru there is a vast gap, as between day and night watch. The guru shows the way to Vaikunth; the sadguru gives his own abode. The sadguru gives his own abode, and the rounds of birth are removed. (This half-line is printed as "shaa inth aan", which is a typesetting corruption and carries no sense as it stands.) One beholds the unbroken Vrindavan. Trikam finds rest in the sadguru's word; the pilgrimage is attained while sitting at home. As between day and night watch, so is the vast gap between guru and sadguru.)

Just as there is a gap between day and night, such is the difference between guru and sadguru. A guru shows us only how to attain a liberated realm such as Vaikunth, while a sadguru — [as the source repeats here] shows how to attain a liberated realm such as Vaikunth. The sadguru, however, shows us his own state, and because of this our rounds of birth and death come to an end. That is, the God who dwells forever, everywhere, as the one, undivided Ram — who dwells in the unbroken Vrindavan — is all that then remains. Trikamdas says that thus, through the sadguru's teaching, we shall enjoy complete peace, and the pilgrimage-place that is the sadguru comes to us while sitting at home itself; hence, just as great as the difference between day and night, that great is the difference between guru and sadguru.

According to the three gunas, whichever of the three types of quality (guna) a given guru possesses, he gives instruction of that same kind; but a sadguru gives instruction in supreme devotion that transcends the three gunas (trigunatit).

Jnani — Knowledge is nothing but a collection of information. (Knowledge itself is nothing other than a mere collection of pieces of information.)

Sant — Apply the information in a known situation; that is understanding. (One who takes whatever knowledge he has and puts it into practice in an available, familiar state or circumstance — such a person is called a sant, a wise and understanding one.)

Guru — Application, diligent and thorough application: to apply the information in an unknown situation. Explication — to develop, to open up, to bring out. (One who applies whatever knowledge he has to unfamiliar circumstances is called a guru — one who gives understanding to the ignorant.)

Sadguru — Skill: to create new information for any situation, whether known or unknown; able to draw up a blueprint. (One who possesses the skill to devise entirely new knowledge suited to any state or condition whatsoever, whether manifest or unmanifest, and to draw up its blueprint — such a one is called a sadguru.)

The sadguru has no need of scriptures, Vedas, Puranas, or bundles of old texts; he himself can bring about wholly new creation, can compose wholly new works, and has no need to search anything out. Searching and seeking is something the knowledgeable, the ignorant, the inquirers, the seekers of some end, and the distressed all have to do. The sadguru, however, need not search for anything at all — he already knows a very great deal. Thus the sadguru is a fully realized being possessing complete power and sovereign glory. Among gurus, some are religious teachers (dharmaguru) and some are teachers of worldly knowledge (vidyaguru); gurus, in this way, each carry a particular quality according to the three gunas. There are base, lowly gurus as well.

If a difference remains between guru and sadguru, one does not attain the Supreme Being; only if the two are brought together as one is the Supreme Being attained. This point is an important one. By way of illustration it is said that the soul, after wandering through the eighty-four [lakh species of birth], finally arrives at God's own court — that is, when true understanding dawns, it lodges a complaint. That complaint concerns the suffering endured in the womb and the torment of the wheel of the ocean of worldly existence (bhavsagar); at that point it says a guru has been obtained, because the soul has now come to true understanding, but God had not yet come to its aid. However, when God himself comes forward of his own accord, in the form of the sadguru, to help it, then all worry over its sufferings comes to an end. After that, the delusion of the world, or the fear of the ocean of worldly existence, comes to an end. A hymn (pad) relating to this illustration has been given in order to make guru and sadguru understood. Further, in order to show guru and sadguru as one and the same, a special exposition has been given in the chapter Nitya Pralay (Daily Dissolution).
